title: Amazon to invest $1 billion over five years in US data center communities
key_facts: Amazon Web Services (AWS, Amazon's cloud-computing division) announced on Friday 2 Oct 2026 an additional $1 billion investment over five years in communities where it builds data centers.
The money is on top of existing commitments and is meant for education, job training, energy affordability, water and energy preservation, and other local priorities.
AWS CEO Matt Garman said in a blog post that the US 'can't afford to lose' the AI race and that a lapse in national focus or resolve could put it behind, 'potentially irreparably so'.
Garman also claimed that foreign nations could be 'intentionally seeding misinformation' about data centers in the US to slow it down; CBS gives no evidence for this claim.
A recent CBS News poll found more Americans oppose than favor data centers in their area, largely over perceived harm to the environment and local resources.
Data Center Watch says 30 states have introduced or adopted legislation or taken other action on data center concerns; some communities imposed moratoriums.
Environment America says grassroots efforts have blocked at least 45 developments in 27 states, valued at $68 billion.
Schneider Electric projects US electricity demand to rise 16% by 2029, mainly because of data centers.
quote_evidence: Amazon's cloud computing division on Friday announced a new effort to temper opposition to data centers in some U.S. communities, while saying the U.S. "can't afford to lose" the race to dominate artificial intelligence globally.

The tech giant pledged to invest an additional $1 billion over five years in the communities where it builds data centers, the facilities that power AI, on top of existing commitments. Amazon said the money will go toward education, job training, energy affordability, and water and energy preservation, and also fund other local priorities.
A recent CBS News poll found that more Americans oppose than favor data centers in their areas, largely because they perceive the facilities as harming the environment and draining local resources.
why_it_matters_hint: A major cloud company is paying for local goodwill because opposition to data centers is growing and, in CBS's words, is blocking or delaying projects.
